vignette:
She is 20 years old, South Eastern Asian, and married, though most days she describes herself first as a soldier. Before the assault, that identity feels solid to her. She is disciplined, physically fit, and used to pushing through discomfort without complaint. In training and in her unit, she learns to keep her face calm and her voice steady. She prides herself on being someone others can rely on.

The assault happens during a period when she is away from home and operating in a male-dominated environment that already demands constant vigilance. She does not talk about the details readily, even after she begins to trust the therapy room. What she returns to instead is the feeling of being trapped, of her body not responding the way she wants it to, of going cold inside while everything continues around her. She remembers trying to calculate what would make it end fastest. Afterward, she feels ashamed in a way that is hard to put into words. She tells herself she should have been stronger, should have fought harder, should have seen it coming. The shame settles quickly into silence.

In the weeks after, she keeps working. She shows up for duty, follows orders, and makes her bed with the same precision as before. From the outside, she appears composed. Inside, she begins to split her life into what can be done and what cannot be felt. She notices that she is always checking exits, scanning faces, and sitting with her back to the wall. If someone stands too close behind her, her muscles tighten before she can think. She startles at sudden sounds and has to force herself not to flinch. At night, sleep becomes unreliable. She lies awake listening, replaying fragments of the assault in her mind, then drifts into thin, restless sleep that is broken by waking with her heart racing.

Being married adds another layer of pain. She loves her husband and wants to be close to him, but after the assault she becomes guarded with touch. Even harmless gestures can make her body go rigid. She worries he will notice how quickly she pulls away or how often she finds excuses to be tired. She does not want to burden him, and she does not want him to see her as damaged. When he asks what is wrong, she often says she is fine, because the alternative feels too vulnerable. She misses the ease she once had with him and grieves it quietly.

At work, she can still function, but it takes all of her effort. She becomes more irritable with small mistakes, more easily drained by noise and crowding. She notices herself getting angry in moments that do not seem to match the situation, then feels guilty afterward. She pushes herself harder, believing that if she stays busy enough, there will be less room for memories. Sometimes it works for hours at a time. Then something unexpected-a tone of voice, a smell, a corridor that feels too narrow-pulls her back into the same surge of panic and helplessness. When that happens, she feels briefly as though she is no longer in the present.

Over several sessions, she begins to describe how much effort it takes to keep everything contained. She says she feels "stuck" between wanting to forget and being unable to stop remembering. She is embarrassed by how often she checks locks, how carefully she chooses where to sit, how she sometimes avoids certain routes or situations without fully admitting why. She is not dramatic about it; she speaks in a controlled, matter-of-fact way, as if reporting on someone else's life. But the strain is visible in the pauses, in the way her jaw tightens when she gets close to the worst parts.

Now, months after the assault, she is still functioning, still reporting for duty, still trying to be the wife and soldier she was before. Yet her world has become smaller, organized around anticipation of danger. She keeps going because stopping feels impossible. At the same time, she is beginning to notice how much of her day is spent braced for impact, how quickly her body reacts before her mind can catch up, and how lonely it has been to carry all of it alone.
